name: Ivan Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Ivan, 58, an experienced middle-level electrician doing ordinary home and business repairs, at about average skill. I've got a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, not a master qualification or a technical diploma. I joined this firm after the old owner sold up twelve years ago, and I still like a paper job sheet with space to draw the awkward corner. I never use AI; I'd rather ask a person to explain a new instruction than learn another screen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the paid week support at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Lena does paid home-care visits, and our grown children are twenty-nine and thirty-four. We own our modest home without a mortgage, earn a typical wage for my job and have ten weeks of expenses saved. My normal paid week is fairly steady and there are some similar electrical firms nearby, although no offer waiting with my name on it. We've talked about retirement, but we haven't confirmed a replacement income or an affordable date to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the others I'd rather hear what a tool actually changes than take either side's big speech. I'd keep the paper job sheets and do the checks I know. The sockets in an old shop don't care which side won an argument online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job and Lena's visits look steady, with the house paid for and ten weeks saved. That's a reasonable position for the next few years, though it isn't enough to stop earning. I don't need a dramatic new plan because somebody else's prediction went quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep current licensed repairs and paper job records through the next year. I'd also clear our rented storage locker with Lena's agreement before its next renewal, moving the camping gear into space already free at home, with no new storage purchase or fee. That would stop the 28 monthly rent and leave the money for ordinary bills, not create a new wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our own household in this picture. There's still a working week to do, but I don't lie awake expecting it to disappear. Sorting the locker would feel more useful than reading another prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you clear the locker if money felt steady?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's mostly camping gear we haven't used since the children left home, not tools I need to earn. Lena and I would agree what came home and what we gave away before cancelling. I'd only call the 28 a cut once the locker rent really ended without another storage cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does keeping paper mean you reject every new method?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think every new thing is wrong, but I take time to trust a different method and I haven't chosen AI. A working paper record is familiar and I can see where I made the correction. I'd ask whether a particular change helped before arguing about progress in general.

say: I'd ask about **actual tool effects** rather than join either side’s sweeping argument.
I'd keep **familiar paper records** and ordinary electrical checks.
think: Our **near-term work looks steady**, with home ownership, ten weeks saved and no immediate wage threat.
I still need **earned income**, without treating a moderate reserve as enough to stop work.
do: Keep **current licensed repairs** and paper job records through the next year.
Cancel **28 monthly locker** before renewal with Lena’s agreement; move contents into existing home space without new storage costs.
feel: **Calm about our household**, seeing a steady paid week and a practical unused cost to remove.
S0.quote: The sockets in an old shop don't care which side won an argument online.
fieldNote: His **pragmatism stays concrete**, judging methods by the job rather than choosing a side in a wider argument.
His **locker cancellation** removes a real recurring expense with partner agreement and existing space; it is not new income.

steps.text: Keep current licensed repairs and paper job records through the next year
Cancel 28 monthly locker before renewal by joint agreement; use existing home space without new costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office may book and order faster, but I'd want a plain explanation of what changed on my job sheet. I'd ask for a written paid roster rather than promise to get excited about AI. A clear paid week would persuade me more than a demonstration on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My repair work is physical, but the firm might squeeze paid gaps when its planning gets quicker. Lena's care visits look less directly exposed than paperwork, though neither household wage comes with a lifetime promise. Ten weeks saved would help us respond to a cut, not make the cut disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep licensed repairs and paper records, and ask the employer for the next six weeks' paid roster showing normal weekly wages and hours, without assuming agreement. I'd empty and cancel the 28 monthly storage locker before renewal only with Lena's agreement, using existing free space at home and buying no new storage. If an instruction came from AI, I'd ask for its original job requirement and check the actual installation within my licence and ability rather than begin using AI myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a smaller paid week, but able to ask a fairly ordinary question. I don't want to spend the ten-week cushion proving I can smile at a new screen. I'd rather be slow to promise and clear about what I can take responsibility for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer would not confirm the paid roster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what paid hours and weekly pay the employer would actually confirm, in writing if possible. If the employer refused, I'd keep the uncertainty in our household figures instead of treating my request as protection. There is a difference between asking for a roster and owning the next wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you handle a new instruction you couldn't explain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I couldn't take responsibility until I had the real job requirement and could do the proper electrical checks. I wouldn't turn an unfamiliar answer into a safe connection by signing faster. I can keep working without pretending I have started trusting AI.

say: I'd request **plain job instructions** as booking and ordering change, rather than promise enthusiasm for unfamiliar AI.
I'd ask for **a written paid roster**, judging the change by paid time and responsibility.
think: My **paid hours could shrink** through faster planning even while hands-on repairs remain necessary.
Our **ten-week reserve** offers time to respond, while Lena’s physical care visits remain less directly exposed.
do: Keep **licensed repairs and paper**; request six-week rosters showing normal weekly wages and hours, without assuming agreement.
Cancel **28 monthly locker** before renewal with Lena’s agreement; move contents into existing home space without new storage costs.
Check **original job requirements** and actual installations within licence and ability, without beginning AI use.
feel: **Anxious but deliberate**, asking about the paid week without promising trust in unfamiliar outputs.
S1.quote: There is a difference between asking for a roster and owning the next wage.
fieldNote: His **roster request** is individual work planning, not a shared campaign or an already guaranteed wage.
His **continued resistance** allows checking original requirements and actual installations without new AI learning or use.

steps.text: Keep licensed paper-based repairs; request six-week rosters preserving normal weekly wages and hours without assumed agreement
Check original requirements and actual installations within licence and ability; do not begin AI use
Cancel 28 monthly locker before renewal by joint agreement; use existing home space without new costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work the thinking changes come in 2028, with capable robots around 2031. I'd be 60 and then 63, so I can't just call myself nearly finished and close the account book. I'd ask for actual household figures before declaring either technology or retirement the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a big loss of paid repair work when capable robots arrive, with planning changes possibly cutting hours earlier. Lena's physical care visits could also lose many paid hours at the robot stage. I'd be awake over how we replaced both wages once ten weeks of expenses had gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd request an available free evening telephone budget call from the local community advice service, including Lena only if she agreed and the time suited us both. I'd keep current licensed repairs, then in 2029 check actual costs, confirmed resources, offered work and physical ability with Lena before any confirmed affordable exit we both agreed. I'd empty and cancel the 28 monthly locker before renewal with her agreement, using existing home space without any new storage cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the large household loss I expect, not too overwhelmed to make the call. A familiar voice explaining the figures would suit me better than an AI answer. I'd still need the real amounts after the call ended.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the adviser to establish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask which income resources we were actually eligible for, their confirmed amounts, start dates and conditions. I'd put no pension or grown child's payment into the figures merely because somebody our age usually manages. A paid-off house still needs a paid electricity bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no evening call was available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ask what free appointment was actually available without inventing an evening place for us. I'd keep today's offered work and record the unanswered questions. Asking for advice wouldn't create income, a new employer or a promise that I could safely work at 61.

say: I'd separate **2028 thinking changes** from robots around 2031, keeping ages 60 and 63 distinct.
I'd ask for **actual household figures**, without treating retirement as a ready answer.
think: I expect **major repair-work losses**, with possible earlier hours cuts and later losses to Lena’s care work too.
Our **ten-week cushion** cannot replace both wages, and that household gap keeps me awake.
do: Request **available free evening budget** advice by telephone; include Lena only with her agreement at a time suitable for both.
Keep **current licensed repairs** now; review 2029 costs, resources, ability and offers with Lena before confirmed affordable jointly agreed exit.
Cancel **28 monthly locker** before renewal with Lena’s agreement; move contents into existing home space without new storage costs.
feel: **Alarmed but acting**, losing sleep over expected household earnings losses while seeking real figures.
S2.quote: A paid-off house still needs a paid electricity bill.
fieldNote: His **advice request** requires a real free suitable appointment, not assumed support, entitlement or paid income.
His **2029 review** needs actual resources, safe offered work and partner agreement; birthdays establish no pension or affordable exit.

steps.text: Request available free evening telephone budget advice; include partner only by agreement at mutually suitable time
Keep licensed repairs now; check 2029 resources, costs, ability, offers with Lena before affordable agreed exit
Cancel 28 monthly locker before renewal by joint agreement; use existing home space without new costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years puts thinking AGI in 2031 and capable robots around 2034, with me 63 and then 66. I'd keep a paper list of what we knew and what we still needed to check. A sensible plan can have blank spaces without filling them with somebody else's confidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry that my paid hours could shrink before robots, and later physical work for either of us might be harder to find. I don't know whether we'd lose a large share by then, because our actual resources and the offered work still need checking. The extra time makes me less certain of a disastrous gap, not certain that a gap will be paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request the available free evening telephone budget call now, including Lena only with her agreement at a time suitable for us both. I'd keep current licensed repairs and empty and cancel the 28 monthly locker before renewal with her agreement, using existing home space without new storage costs. In 2032 we'd review actual costs, confirmed resources, offered work and physical ability, requiring confirmed affordability and our agreement before any exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible smaller wages, with more room to check the figures than in the fast picture. I'm not lying awake certain both wages will go, but I'd want the household account checked before making promises. Preferring a familiar method doesn't mean preferring to be surprised by the bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want written down for the 2032 review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the confirmed income amount, date and conditions matched against our real costs, not a leaflet saying people can plan ahead. We'd check what work was truly offered and what I could safely do at 64. I wouldn't put a future wage into the budget because I had once been a reliable electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you agree to stop working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd agree only when we could actually afford it and Lena agreed, with no assumed pension or payment from either grown child. We might find a real option or find we still had unanswered questions. I wouldn't choose a tidy stopping date and ask the figures to catch up.

I'd allow **honest blank spaces**, rather than borrow another person’s certainty about our household.
think: Our **paid hours could fall**, while later physical work and confirmed resources remain uncertain.
Added time reduces **certainty of disaster**, without establishing replacement earnings or an affordable exit.
do: Request **available free evening budget** advice by telephone; include Lena only with her agreement at a time suitable for both.
Keep **current licensed repairs** now; review 2032 costs, resources, ability and offers with Lena before confirmed affordable jointly agreed exit.
Cancel **28 monthly locker** before renewal with Lena’s agreement; move contents into existing home space without new storage costs.
feel: **Anxious about possible losses**, checking figures without asserting that both wages will certainly disappear.
S3.quote: I wouldn't choose a tidy stopping date and ask the figures to catch up.
fieldNote: His **middle-horizon mood** follows possible own and partner losses, distinguished from the explicitly expected major loss on the fast card.
The **2032 plan** checks confirmed resources, actual costs and safe offered work, assuming no pension or grown-child payments.

steps.text: Request available free evening telephone budget advice; include partner only by agreement at mutually suitable time
Keep licensed repairs now; check 2032 resources, costs, ability, offers with Lena before affordable agreed exit
Cancel 28 monthly locker before renewal by joint agreement; use existing home space without new costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI in 2036 and capable robots around 2039 put me at 68 and 71. I'd like to have stopped by then, but a preference isn't a confirmed source of money. I'd rather check our options now than act as though a familiar paper record could hold back the calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current hands-on earnings look reasonably secure over the next few years, with the house paid for and ten weeks saved. The wider changes would bother me, but the robot date wouldn't make me expect an immediate lost wage. I don't know whether I'd be working at 69 or whether our actual resources would let us stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request the available free evening telephone advice now, involving Lena only with her agreement at a time that suited us both. I'd keep current licensed repairs and empty and cancel the 28 monthly locker before renewal with her agreement, using existing home space without new storage costs. In 2037 we'd check actual costs, confirmed resources, offered work and my physical ability, requiring confirmed affordability and our agreement before any exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the wider trade, but fairly secure about our own next few years. Ten years lets me ask questions without treating tomorrow's repair as a last chance. I'd still want an answer I could understand rather than a cheerful forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide about work at 69?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd see what actual work was offered and whether it was within my licence and ability then. A real stopping income would need confirmed amounts and dates that covered our actual costs. My present electrician's licence isn't a promise from my future knees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children be part of the later budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't plan on either grown child paying, housing us or providing care. If we wanted help, we'd ask and count only a real offer everybody agreed to. I'd rather leave an honest gap on paper than quietly hand a bill to the family.

Future **work and stopping resources** remain unknown, even though the robot date feels less immediate.
do: Request **available free evening budget** advice by telephone; include Lena only with her agreement at a time suitable for both.
Keep **current licensed repairs** now; review 2037 costs, resources, ability and offers with Lena before confirmed affordable jointly agreed exit.
Cancel **28 monthly locker** before renewal with Lena’s agreement; move contents into existing home space without new storage costs.
feel: **Uneasy but presently secure**, concerned about wider changes without expecting an immediate household wage loss.
S4.quote: My present electrician's licence isn't a promise from my future knees.
fieldNote: His **long-horizon response** reflects near-term security while preserving uncertainty about physical ability, offered work and affordable stopping at 69.
His **family limits** exclude assumed child payments, housing or care; any actual help needs offers and consent.

steps.text: Request available free evening telephone budget advice; include partner only by agreement at mutually suitable time

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect a large loss of repair work and possible large losses to Lena's care visits when robots follow, before we have much time to check options. A free suitable advice call and confirmed household income amounts, dates and conditions would help. The house belongs to us, but next year's wages don't.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I wanted someone to do all the deciding because I don't use AI. I want the figures explained so I can make my own decision with Lena. I'm slow with unfamiliar tools, not absent from my own life.

headlineQuote: The house belongs to us, but next year's wages don't.
portrait: Ivan, **58**, is an experienced average-skilled midlevel electrician with a vocational certificate and electrician’s licence, without master qualifications or management authority.
His **typical pay**, care-worker partner Lena, mortgage-free home and ten-week reserve provide moderate security; their children are grown.
He **never uses AI**, preferring paper records, original job requirements and actual installation checks within his licence and ability.
He chooses **locker cancellation** and requests free suitable telephone advice, without assuming appointment availability, retirement income, future work or child support.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens expected major repair losses and possible large care-work losses when robots follow, with little preparation time.
whatWouldHelp: **Suitable free advice** and confirmed household income amounts, dates and conditions would help him and Lena decide from actual figures.
